topic.name: Graphing Cubic Curves Containing One Distinct Real Root

question.text:
Given that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x)=-x^3-3x^2-4x-2,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+1)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+1)$ using synthetic division: \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrr} & x^3 & x^2 &x^1 & x^0 \\ {\color{red}{-1}} & -1 & -3 & -4 & -2 \\ & & 1 & 2 & 2 \\ \hline & -1 & -2 & -2 & 0 \end{array} \]

Therefore, \begin{align*} \dfrac{f(x)}{x+1} &= -x^2 -2x - 2 \\[5pt] &= -(x^2+2x+2), \end{align*}

which means that \[ f(x) = -(x+1)(x^2 +2x +2). \]

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $x^2 +2x +2=0$ is

\[ \mathcal{D}= 2^2 - 4(1)(2) = -4 < 0, \] which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=-1.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

\[ y = -(0)^3-3(0)^2-4(0)-2 = -2 \]

So, the curve:

  • has a $y$-intercept at $(0,-2),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-1,$ and

  • has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph has an ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

question.text:
Given that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x) = x^3 + x^2 + 3 x + 3,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+1)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+1)$ using synthetic division: \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrr} & x^3 & x^2 &x^1 & x^0 \\ {\color{red}{-1}} & 1 & 1 & 3 & 3 \\ & & -1 & 0 & -3 \\ \hline &1 & 0 & 3 & 0 \end{array} \]

Therefore,

\[ \dfrac{f(x)}{x+1} = x^2 + 3 \]

which means that \[ f(x) = (x+1)(x^2 + 3). \]

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $x^2 + 3 = 0$ is \[ \mathcal{D}= 0^2 - 4(1)(3) = -12 < 0, \] which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=-1.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

\begin{align*} y &= 0^3 + 0^2 + 3(0) + 3 = 3. \end{align*}

So, the curve:

  • has a $y$-intercept at $(0,3),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-1,$ and

  • has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

question.text:
Given that $x$ is a factor of $f(x)= -x^3 - 2 x^2 - 4 x,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, let's factor the polynomial. We factor out a common factor $-x,$ as follows: \begin{align} f(x) & = -x^3 - 2x^2 - 4x\\[3pt] & = -x(x^2 + 2x + 4) \end{align}

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $x^2 +2x + 4=0$ is \[ \mathcal{D}= 2^2 - 4(1)(4) = -12 < 0, \] which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=0.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

\[ y = -0^3 - 2 (0)^2 - 4(0) = 0 \]

So, the curve:

  • has a $y$-intercept at $(0,0),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=0,$ and

  • has no more $x$-intercepts.
